newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia ex-prosecutor denies being "U.S. puppet".
newsitem.headline: Colombia ex-prosecutor denies being "U.S. puppet".

text.p: Colombia's former chief prosecutor, who quit his post last week to prepare a bid for the presidency, rejected criticism that he was a puppet of the United States, in a newspaper interview on Sunday.
Alfonso Valdivieso, who resigned last Thursday after two-and-a-half years as the nation's top lawman, has been accused by his critics in Congress of "bowing to the whims of U.S. imperialism."

He became a firm favorite with Washington for his crusade against corruption in the upper echelons of Colombian politics and for his outspoken support for tougher anti-drug measures, including the so-far unsuccessful move to lift Colombia's six-year ban on extradition.

"The argument has been perversely twisted ... There has not been a single expression by the chief prosecutor's office that was due to pressure from the United States," Valdivieso told the respected regional El Pais newspaper.

The day after Valdivieso's resignation, U.S. ambassador to Bogota, Myles Frechette, said he had lost an "ally" in the prosecutor's office but, in what was interpreted as a gesture of tacit support, wished the outgoing official the "best of luck" for the presidential elections in May 1998.
Valdivieso, a member of the ruling Liberal Party, has consistently come out ahead in national polls of voter preferences.

He has, however, shunned the backing of his party leadership and said he will run as an independent -- a move that threatens to end a long-standing tradition of two-party politics where Liberals and Conservatives alternated in power.
"I'm not calling on the party machinery. Quite the contrary, I'm ignoring it and even challenging it. Now is not the time for party politics," Valdivieso told El Pais.
In a forceful rebuttal to his critics, Valdivieso also accused President Ernesto Samper of caving in to U.S. pressures.
"The government's actions against drug crop cultivation, trafficking and other drug issues were largely the product of U.S. pressure," the former chief prosecutor said.

Valdivieso's relationship with Samper, and other former senior politicians, has been rocky at best. He earned many public enemies by heading the so-called 8,000 Process, which investigated claims that Samper financed his 1994 election campaign with millions of dollars of cocaine cash.
